title: Foundations: Psychological Horror - The Complete Guide
summary: What Psychological Horror books are, where the genre came from, and how to read them.
body:
Psychological Horror: Horror is the literature of fear: stories that make the skin crawl by making the impossible feel present. Poe mapped the territory; Stoker, Shelley, and Lovecraft built its great houses.

History: The Gothic novel (1764) fathered horror; Poe's tales (1830s-40s) perfected it. Dracula (1897) and Frankenstein (1818) are its twin peaks; M. R. James and Lovecraft defined the 20th-century ghost and cosmic modes.

HOW TO READ THIS SHELF: start with the landmark titles below — each record carries the complete plot, themes, a quoted passage, and craft notes. Read foundations first, then follow the ladder: compounded titles deepen the form, advanced titles challenge it.

title: The Turn of the Screw (1898) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for The Turn of the Screw by Henry James (1898): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Turn of the Screw by Henry James (1898). Shelf fit: The ghost story as ambiguity.

COMPLETE PLOT: A governess sees two figures at a country estate and believes they are corrupting the children. Are the ghosts real, or is she mad? James never says.

THEMES: Ambiguity as the purest horror.

FROM THE TEXT: "The story had held us, round the fire, sufficiently breathless."

CRAFT NOTE: James's frame narrative doubles the uncertainty - horror as interpretation.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PSYCHOLOGICAL HORROR SHELF: The ghost story as ambiguity. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: The Monkey's Paw (1902) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for The Monkey's Paw by W. W. Jacobs (1902): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Monkey's Paw by W. W. Jacobs (1902). Shelf fit: Be careful what you wish for.

COMPLETE PLOT: The White family gets three wishes from a mummified paw. They wish for money - and receive it as compensation for their son's death. The final wish, as something knocks at the door, is left to the reader's dread.

THEMES: Irony as horror; the wish as trap.

FROM THE TEXT: "It had a spell put on it by an old fakir."

CRAFT NOTE: Jacobs's three-wish structure is horror's most imitated machine.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PSYCHOLOGICAL HORROR SHELF: Be careful what you wish for. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

Dagon by H. P. Lovecraft (1919). Shelf fit: The sea horror.

THEMES: The ocean as the unconscious.

FROM THE TEXT: "Lovecraft's signature: the narrator who cannot unsee."

title: The Fall of the House of Usher (1839) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for The Fall of the House of Usher by Edgar Allan Poe (1839): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Fall of the House of Usher by Edgar Allan Poe (1839). Shelf fit: The house as patient.

COMPLETE PLOT: The narrator visits Roderick Usher in his decaying mansion; Roderick's sister Madeline is entombed alive, and when she returns, the house itself splits and sinks into the tarn.

THEMES: Decay as destiny; the building as body.

FROM THE TEXT: "The house of Usher seemed to include both the family and the family mansion."

CRAFT NOTE: Poe fuses setting and psychology - the house is the mind.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PSYCHOLOGICAL HORROR SHELF: The house as patient. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde by Robert Louis Stevenson (1886): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde by Robert Louis Stevenson (1886). Shelf fit: The divided self.

COMPLETE PLOT: Utterson investigates his friend Jekyll's will leaving everything to the repellent Hyde - and discovers they are one man, chemistry having split respectability from appetite.

THEMES: Respectability vs. appetite.

FROM THE TEXT: "All human beings are commingled out of good and evil."

CRAFT NOTE: Stevenson's London fog is the divided mind made weather.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PSYCHOLOGICAL HORROR SHELF: The divided self. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

summary: Full record for Dracula by Bram Stoker (1897): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Dracula by Bram Stoker (1897). Shelf fit: The vampire novel.

COMPLETE PLOT: Count Dracula buys English property and sails to Whitby in a box of earth; Jonathan Harker, Mina, Lucy, Van Helsing and company hunt him across Europe with phonograph diaries and typewritten logs, finally staking him in Transylvania.

THEMES: Modernity vs. ancient evil; documented horror.

FROM THE TEXT: "Listen to them, the children of the night. What music they make!"

CRAFT NOTE: Stoker's epistolary collage - letters, diaries, clippings - makes the unreal documented.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PSYCHOLOGICAL HORROR SHELF: The vampire novel. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: Frankenstein (1818) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for Frankenstein by Mary Shelley (1818): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Frankenstein by Mary Shelley (1818). Shelf fit: Horror's founding text.

COMPLETE PLOT: Victor Frankenstein's Creature, abandoned at birth, learns to read Paradise Lost and demands a mate; refused, he murders Victor's brother, friend, and bride. The chase ends among Arctic ice, creator and created destroying each other.

THEMES: The horror of irresponsibility.

FROM THE TEXT: "I am malicious because I am miserable."

CRAFT NOTE: Shelley's horror is moral: the monster is made, not born.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PSYCHOLOGICAL HORROR SHELF: Horror's founding text. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: The Tell-Tale Heart (1843) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for The Tell-Tale Heart by Edgar Allan Poe (1843): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Tell-Tale Heart by Edgar Allan Poe (1843). Shelf fit: Guilt as horror.

COMPLETE PLOT: A narrator insists on his sanity while describing the perfect murder of an old man - dismemberment, floorboards - undone by the hallucinated beating of the victim's heart. Two pages; no wasted word.

THEMES: Guilt as the real haunting.

FROM THE TEXT: "It is the beating of his hideous heart!"

CRAFT NOTE: Poe's first-person madness: the narrator condemns himself.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PSYCHOLOGICAL HORROR SHELF: Guilt as horror. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Themes: Guilt as the real haunting.

summary: Full record for The Call of Cthulhu by H. P. Lovecraft (1928): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Call of Cthulhu by H. P. Lovecraft (1928). Shelf fit: Cosmic horror's founding document.

COMPLETE PLOT: Francis Thurston pieces together his uncle's notes: a worldwide cult, a sunken city, and the dreaming god Cthulhu. The horror is scale: humanity is incidental.

THEMES: The universe is indifferent; knowledge is dangerous.

FROM THE TEXT: "That is not dead which can eternal lie."

CRAFT NOTE: Lovecraft's documentary collage makes the impossible feel filed and factual.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PSYCHOLOGICAL HORROR SHELF: Cosmic horror's founding document. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: The Great God Pan (1894) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for The Great God Pan by Arthur Machen (1894): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Great God Pan by Arthur Machen (1894). Shelf fit: Victorian decadence horror.

COMPLETE PLOT: Dr. Raymond's brain surgery on Mary lets her see the god Pan; years later, her daughter Helen Vaughan leaves a trail of suicides and corruption through London society. The horror is never shown - only its effects.

THEMES: The veil between worlds; suggestion over spectacle.

FROM THE TEXT: "Machen's rule: describe the reaction, never the monster."

CRAFT NOTE: Machen's rule: describe the reaction, never the monster.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PSYCHOLOGICAL HORROR SHELF: Victorian decadence horror. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

summary: Full record for Carmilla by J. Sheridan Le Fanu (1872): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Carmilla by J. Sheridan Le Fanu (1872). Shelf fit: The vampire novella, before Dracula.

COMPLETE PLOT: Laura, isolated in a Styrian castle, is visited by the beautiful Carmilla - intimate, strange, nocturnal. The revelation: Carmilla is the centuries-dead Countess Karnstein, preying on Laura's family for generations.

THEMES: Intimacy as predation; the familiar made strange.

FROM THE TEXT: "You are mine, you shall be mine, you and I are one for ever."

CRAFT NOTE: Le Fanu's dream-logic dread taught Stoker everything.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PSYCHOLOGICAL HORROR SHELF: The vampire novella, before Dracula. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Shelf fit: The vampire novella, before Dracula.
Themes: Intimacy as predation; the familiar made strange.
